Arsenic.plain: Arsenic occurs naturally in bedrock across much of New England — it is not usually a pollution problem, it is a geology problem. It is especially common in granite country.
Arsenic.effect: Some people who drink water containing arsenic in excess of the maximum contaminant level over many years could experience skin damage or problems with their circulatory system, and may have an increased risk of getting cancer.
Arsenic.source: U.S. EPA, mandatory health effects language — Arsenic
Arsenic.who: Risk builds over years of exposure rather than suddenly.
Arsenic.name: Arsenic

Copper.plain: Copper, like lead, usually comes from the plumbing rather than the source — most often from copper pipe and its fittings, especially where water sits still.
Copper.effect: Copper is an essential nutrient, but some people who drink water containing copper in excess of the action level over a relatively short amount of time could experience gastrointestinal distress. Some people who drink water containing copper in excess of the action level over many years could suffer liver or kidney damage.
Copper.source: U.S. EPA, mandatory health effects language — Lead and Copper Rule
Copper.who: People with Wilson's disease should consult their doctor.
Copper.name: Copper

Benzene.plain: Benzene is an industrial solvent, and also reaches groundwater from leaking fuel storage tanks and landfills.
Benzene.effect: Some people who drink water containing benzene in excess of the maximum contaminant level over many years could experience anemia or a decrease in blood platelets, and may have an increased risk of getting cancer.
Benzene.source: U.S. EPA, mandatory health effects language — Benzene
Benzene.name: Benzene

Antimony, Total.plain: Antimony reaches water from petroleum refineries, fire retardants, ceramics, electronics and solder.
Antimony, Total.effect: Some people who drink water containing antimony well in excess of the maximum contaminant level over many years could experience increases in blood cholesterol and decreases in blood sugar.
Antimony, Total.source: U.S. EPA, mandatory health effects language — Antimony
Antimony, Total.name: Antimony, Total

Beryllium, Total.plain: Beryllium enters water from metal refineries, coal-burning factories and electrical works, and from natural deposits.
Beryllium, Total.effect: Some people who drink water containing beryllium well in excess of the maximum contaminant level over many years could develop intestinal lesions.
Beryllium, Total.source: U.S. EPA, mandatory health effects language — Beryllium
Beryllium, Total.name: Beryllium, Total

Gross Alpha, Excl. Radon and U.plain: Gross alpha is a screening measurement rather than a single substance. It counts alpha-particle radioactivity from naturally occurring elements in rock, and a high reading prompts testing for the specific ones.
Gross Alpha, Excl. Radon and U.effect: Certain minerals are radioactive and may emit a form of radiation known as alpha radiation. Some people who drink water containing alpha emitters in excess of the maximum contaminant level over many years may have an increased risk of getting cancer.
Gross Alpha, Excl. Radon and U.source: U.S. EPA, mandatory health effects language — Radionuclides
Gross Alpha, Excl. Radon and U.name: Gross Alpha, Excl. Radon and U

Lead.plain: Lead is almost never in water at its source. It gets picked up on the way to the tap — from the service line under the street, from solder in older joints, from the brass in the tap itself. That makes it a property of your building more than of your town.
Lead.effect: Infants and children who drink water containing lead in excess of the action level could experience delays in their physical or mental development. Children could show slight deficits in attention span and learning abilities. Adults who drink this water over many years could develop kidney problems or high blood pressure.
Lead.source: U.S. EPA, mandatory health effects language — Lead and Copper Rule
Lead.name: Lead

Lead and Copper Rule.name: Lead and Copper Rule
Lead and Copper Rule.plain: The rule governing lead and copper monitoring and corrosion control. A violation is often procedural — a missed sampling round or a late report.

Revised Total Coliform Rule.plain: Coliforms are bacteria that are mostly harmless in themselves. They are measured as an indicator: if they are present, the system may be open to something that is not harmless.
Revised Total Coliform Rule.effect: Coliforms are bacteria that are naturally present in the environment and are used as an indicator that other, potentially harmful, waterborne pathogens may be present or that a potential pathway exists through which contamination may enter the drinking water distribution system.
Revised Total Coliform Rule.source: U.S. EPA, mandatory health effects language — Revised Total Coliform Rule
Revised Total Coliform Rule.who: A warning sign rather than a harm in itself.
Revised Total Coliform Rule.name: Revised Total Coliform Rule

LEAD AND COPPER RULE REVISIONS.name: LEAD AND COPPER RULE REVISIONS
LEAD AND COPPER RULE REVISIONS.plain: A requirement about how a system must monitor for lead and copper, inventory its service lines, and act when results are high. A violation here is usually a failure to do the required work on schedule rather than a measured exceedance.

Nitrate.plain: Nitrate usually comes from fertiliser run-off, septic systems, or manure. It is most common in farming areas and in shallow wells.
Nitrate.effect: Infants below the age of six months who drink water containing nitrate in excess of the maximum contaminant level could become seriously ill and, if untreated, may die. Symptoms include shortness of breath and blue-baby syndrome.
Nitrate.source: U.S. EPA, mandatory health effects language — Nitrate
Nitrate.who: Infants under six months. This is the fastest-acting risk on this list.
Nitrate.name: Nitrate
